subject: math
title: Equations and Inequalities: Linear Equations, Formulas, Inequalities, and Systems
objectives: You will solve one-step and multi-step linear equations, including equations with parentheses, fractions, and variables on both sides.
You will solve a formula (literal equation) for a named letter and use it to find a value.
You will solve linear inequalities, reversing the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number, and graph the solutions on a number line.
You will translate word problems into equations and inequalities, solve them, and answer the question that was asked.
You will solve systems of two linear equations by graphing, substitution, and elimination, and check the solution in both equations.

slides.title: Week 8 Math: Equations and Inequalities
slides.board:
Equations and Inequalities

Linear Equations, Formulas, Inequalities, and Systems

  • Solve one-step and multi-step equations
  • Solve a formula for one of its letters
  • Solve inequalities and graph them on a number line
  • Turn word problems into equations and inequalities
  • Solve systems of two equations

Today: warm-up, equations, formulas, inequalities, word problems, systems, GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 8. Last week you learned to simplify expressions; this week we put an equal sign in the middle and solve. Solving equations is the single most tested algebra skill on the GED math test, and it shows up inside geometry, percent, and data questions too. The good news is that one routine handles almost everything today, and every answer can be checked by plugging it back in. Same plan as always: I teach a rule, show a worked example, we do some together, and then you try some on your own while I watch the clock.
ask: When you hear "solve for x," what do you picture? (expected answer: any; listen for "get x by itself" and build on it)
notes.watch: Pacing for 60 minutes: warm-up 4 min (slide 2); equations 14 min (slides 3–9); formulas 4 min (slides 10–11); inequalities 10 min (slides 12–15); word problems 7 min (slides 16–18); systems 17 min (slides 19–25); strategy and recap 4 min (slides 26–27). If you fall behind, assign the third example on systems (slide 22) as homework and shorten the we-do slides.

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 7 Review
slides.board:
Last week: expressions. Work on paper.

  1. Evaluate 3a − 2b when a = −2 and b = 5.
  2. Simplify 4(x − 3) + 2x.
  3. Simplify 5x − (2x − 7).
  4. Factor 6x + 15.
  5. Is x = 4 a solution of 3x − 5 = 7?
steps: 3. 5x − 2x + 7 = 3x + 7 (the minus sign changes both terms in the parentheses)
5. 3(4) − 5 = 12 − 5 = 7, and 7 = 7. Yes, x = 4 makes the equation true.

notes.say: These are last week's skills, and every one of them comes back today. Distributing and combining like terms are the first moves in solving an equation, and substituting a value is how you check an answer. Take about three minutes, then read me your answers.
ask: What did you get for number 3, and why? (expected answer: 3x + 7; subtracting the parentheses changes the sign of both 2x and −7)
In number 5, what does it mean that x = 4 is a "solution"? (expected answer: it makes both sides equal)
notes.watch: Number 3 is the one to watch: 3x − 7 means the student subtracted only the 2x. Number 5 is the bridge to today: use it to define solution as a value that makes the equation true.

slides.title: An Equation Is a Balance
slides.board:
Solve = find the value that makes the equation true. Do the same thing to both sides.

To undo…do this to both sidesExample
+ 6subtract 6x + 6 = 10 → x = 4
− 6add 6x − 6 = 10 → x = 16
× 6divide by 66x = 30 → x = 5
÷ 6multiply by 6x/6 = 3 → x = 18

Two steps: undo + and − first, then × and ÷. Always check.

notes.say: Picture a balance scale with the same weight on each side. If you take 6 off the left, you have to take 6 off the right, or the scale tips. Solving means peeling layers off the variable with inverse operations: operations that undo each other. When there are two layers, like 3x + 8, peel them in reverse order: the + 8 was done last, so undo it first, then divide by 3.
ask: To solve x − 9 = −4, what do you do to both sides? (expected answer: add 9, so x = 5)
In 3x + 8 = 29, which do you undo first, the 8 or the 3? (expected answer: the + 8, by subtracting 8)
notes.watch: Some adults "move" numbers across the equal sign and forget to change the operation (x − 9 = −4 becomes x = −13). Insist on writing the operation on both sides for the first few problems.

slides.title: Two-Step Equations
slides.board:
Solve each equation and check.

(a) 5x + 12 = −23

(b) n/4 − 6 = 3

notes.say: Watch the order: first the number that is added or subtracted, then the number that multiplies or divides. In part (a), the answer is negative, and that is fine. In part (b), the variable is divided by 4, so we multiply by 4 to undo it. The check takes ten seconds and catches almost every sign error.
ask: In (a), what is −35 divided by 5? (expected answer: −7)
In (b), why do we multiply by 4 instead of dividing? (expected answer: n is divided by 4, and multiplying undoes dividing)
notes.watch: In (a), a student who adds 12 gets 5x = −11. In (b), a student who divides by 4 gets 9/4. Ask: "What operation is attached to the variable right now?"

slides.title: The Multi-Step Routine
slides.board:
1. Simplify each side: distribute, combine like terms, clear fractions.
  2. Variables to one side (subtract the smaller variable term).
  3. Numbers to the other side.
  4. Divide by the coefficient.
  5. Check in the original equation.

Answers can be fractions: 4x = 25 → x = 25/4 = 6.25.

Special cases: the variable drops out and you get a false statement (3 = 7) → no solution; a true statement (5 = 5) → infinitely many solutions.

notes.say: This five-step routine is the backbone of today. Say it with me: simplify, variables to one side, numbers to the other, divide, check. Step 1 is last week's work: distribute and combine like terms on each side separately, without crossing the equal sign. In step 2, subtract the smaller variable term so you avoid negative coefficients when you can. Once in a while, the variables cancel completely. If what is left is false, no number works; if it is true, every number works.
ask: What is the first step in 2(x + 3) = 14? (expected answer: distribute to get 2x + 6 = 14, or divide both sides by 2 to get x + 3 = 7; both give x = 4)
notes.watch: The most common error is distributing to only the first term: 3(x − 4) written as 3x − 4. Have the student draw an arrow from the 3 to each term inside.

slides.title: Variables on Both Sides
slides.board:
Solve and check:

5(x − 3) + 2x = 4x + 9
steps: Combine like terms on the left: 7x − 15 = 4x + 9

notes.say: Follow the routine line by line. Distribute the 5 to both terms, then combine 5x and 2x. Now there are x-terms on both sides, so subtract the smaller one, 4x, from both sides. From there it is a two-step equation. For the check, work each side of the original equation separately; they should match.
ask: Why subtract 4x and not 7x? (expected answer: 4x is smaller, so the x-term stays positive)
What does each side equal when x = 8? (expected answer: 41)
notes.watch: Watch for 5x − 3 in the first line (distributing only to x). That error leads to x = 4, which fails the check: 5(1) + 8 = 13, but 4(4) + 9 = 25.

slides.title: Clearing Fractions
slides.board:
Solve:

3x/4 − 2 = x/2 + 1

Tip: multiply every term by the least common denominator (LCD).
steps: The denominators are 4 and 2, so the LCD is 4.

notes.say: Fractions make many adults nervous, so get rid of them at the start. Multiply every single term on both sides by the LCD, including the whole numbers 2 and 1. After that line, there are no fractions left, and it is an ordinary equation. Decimals work the same way: multiply by 10 or 100, or simply use the calculator on the calculator part of the test.
ask: What happens to the −2 when we multiply every term by 4? (expected answer: it becomes −8)
notes.watch: The trap is multiplying only the fractions: 3x − 2 = 2x + 1 gives x = 3, which fails the check. Have the student draw an arrow from the 4 to every term.

slides.title: Equations Together
slides.board:
Tell me each step before I reveal it.

  1. 4x − 7 = 21
  2. 3(2x + 1) = 5x − 4
  3. x/3 + 5 = x/2
  4. 2(x + 4) = 2x + 5

notes.say: We do these together. For each one, tell me the first move and why, and I will reveal the line. Number 4 is the surprise of the day: the x-terms cancel. Do not panic; read what is left. A false statement means no value of x can ever make the two sides equal.
ask: In number 2, what do you get after distributing? (expected answer: 6x + 3)
In number 3, what do you multiply by? (expected answer: 6, the LCD of 3 and 2)
In number 4, could any number work? (expected answer: no; 2x + 8 is always 3 more than 2x + 5)
notes.watch: In number 2, 6x + 1 means the 3 did not multiply the 1. In number 3, x = 5 usually means the 5 was not multiplied by 6 (2x + 5 = 3x). In number 4, some students write "x = 0"; ask them to check: 2(4) = 8 but 2(0) + 5 = 5.

slides.title: Your Turn: Equations
slides.board:
Three minutes. Work on paper and check each answer.

  1. 7 − 2x = 15
  2. 6x − 4 = 2x + 18
  3. 0.4x + 1.2 = 3.6
  4. −3(x − 2) = 4x − 8

notes.say: Your turn. I am starting the clock for three minutes. Use the routine and check each answer by substituting. When time is up, read me your four answers and tell me which one you checked.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: −4, 5.5, 6, 2)
notes.answer: (1) −2x = 8, so x = −4   (2) 4x = 22, so x = 5.5   (3) 0.4x = 2.4, so x = 6   (4) −3x + 6 = 4x − 8; 14 = 7x; x = 2. Check: −3(0) = 0 and 4(2) − 8 = 0 ✓
notes.watch: Number 1: x = 4 means the negative sign on −2x was dropped. Number 2: x = 3.5 means 18 − 4 instead of 18 + 4. Number 4: −3x − 6 means the student did not multiply two negatives; that leads to x = 2/7.

slides.title: Solving a Formula for a Letter
slides.board:
A literal equation has several letters. "Solve for w" = get w alone.

Use the same moves. Treat every other letter like a number.

FormulaSolved for…
d = rtt = d/r
A = (1/2)bhh = 2A/b
y = mx + bx = (y − b)/m
I = Prtr = I/(Pt)

notes.say: Formulas are equations with letters instead of numbers. If you can solve 3x + 2 = 11, you can solve y = mx + b for x: the moves are identical. Ask yourself, "What is being done to the letter I want, and in what order?" Then undo it in reverse order. This matters on the GED because the formula sheet gives you formulas in one form, and the question often needs a different letter.
ask: To solve d = rt for r, what do you do? (expected answer: divide both sides by t, so r = d/t)
notes.watch: Students often divide only one term: from 3y = 12 − 2x they write y = 4 − 2x. Every term on that side must be divided by 3: y = 4 − (2/3)x.

slides.title: Solve, Then Use, a Formula
slides.board:
The perimeter of a rectangle is P = 2l + 2w.

(a) Solve for w.

(b) Find the width when P = 46 feet and l = 14 feet.
steps: (a) w is multiplied by 2, then 2l is added. Undo the addition first: P − 2l = 2w

notes.say: First we solve the formula, then we use it. Notice that the steps in part (a) are exactly the steps you would use on 46 = 28 + 2w. Writing the formula for w first is useful when you need to find the width for many different rectangles, which is how spreadsheets and pricing tools work.
ask: What would you get if you divided only P by 2? (expected answer: P/2 − 2l, which is wrong; both terms must be divided)
notes.watch: Watch for (P − l)/2. The formula has 2l, so subtract 2l, not l.

notes.say: An inequality has a whole range of answers instead of one. You solve it with the same moves as an equation, with one extra rule. Look at 2 < 5. Multiply both sides by −1 and you get −2 and −5, but now −2 is the bigger number, so the sign has to turn around. That is the flip rule. On the graph, an open dot means the endpoint is not included, and a closed dot means it is. If you write the answer with x on the left, the symbol points the way to shade.
ask: Do you flip the sign in 4x < −12? (expected answer: no; you divide by positive 4, so x < −3)
Open or closed dot for x ≥ 5? (expected answer: closed)
notes.watch: Two opposite mistakes: forgetting to flip when dividing by a negative, and flipping just because the answer or the right side is negative. Only the sign of the number you multiply or divide by matters.

notes.say: The first move is the same as in an equation. The second move divides by negative 3, so the sign flips from greater-than-or-equal to less-than-or-equal. Then I test one number inside the shading and one outside. If the inside number works and the outside number fails, the graph is right. This two-number check is the fastest way to catch a missed flip.
ask: What would the answer be if we forgot to flip? (expected answer: x ≥ −4)
Does x = −4 itself work? (expected answer: yes; 7 + 12 = 19, and 19 ≥ 19)
notes.watch: If the student shades right, have them test x = 0 in the original. It gives 7 ≥ 19, which is false, so the right side cannot be the solution.

figure.alt: Number line from negative 6 to 6 with an open dot at negative 2, a closed dot at 4, and shading between them.

steps: 1. 2x < 12, so x < 6: open dot at 6, shade left.
2. −2x < 8. Divide by −2 and flip: x > −4: open dot at −4, shade right.
3. Divide by positive 4, no flip: x ≥ −5: closed dot at −5, shade right.
4. Subtract 1 from all three parts: −4 < 2x ≤ 8. Divide by 2: −2 < x ≤ 4: open dot at −2, closed dot at 4, shade between.

notes.say: For each one, tell me two things before I reveal it: do we flip, and is the dot open or closed? Number 3 is a trap on purpose: the right side is negative, but we divide by positive 4, so nothing flips. Number 4 is a compound inequality, a "between" statement. Whatever you do, do it to all three parts.
ask: In number 2, do we flip? (expected answer: yes, we divide by −2)
In number 3, do we flip? (expected answer: no, we divide by positive 4)
notes.answer: (1) x < 6, open at 6, left   (2) x > −4, open at −4, right   (3) x ≥ −5, closed at −5, right   (4) −2 < x ≤ 4, open at −2, closed at 4, between
notes.watch: A student who answers x ≤ −5 on number 3 flipped because of the negative 20. Ask: "What number did you divide by? Was it negative?"

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Inequalities
slides.board:
Which inequality is the solution of the inequality below?

6 − 4x ≤ 26

A. x ≤ −5    B. x ≥ −5    C. x ≥ −8    D. x ≤ 5
steps: Eliminate A (x ≤ −5): it comes from dividing −4x ≤ 20 by −4 without flipping the sign. Dividing by a negative flips ≤ to ≥.
Eliminate C (x ≥ −8): it comes from adding 6 instead of subtracting it (−4x ≤ 32). To undo + 6, subtract 6.
Eliminate D (x ≤ 5): it comes from dividing by positive 4 and losing the negative sign on x. The coefficient is −4.
B (x ≥ −5) is correct: 6 − 4x ≤ 26 → −4x ≤ 20 → divide by −4 and flip → x ≥ −5. Check x = 0: 6 ≤ 26 ✓.

notes.say: Here is a GED-style question. Every wrong choice is the result of a real mistake, so matching a choice is not proof. Solve it first, then test one value. Zero is the easiest test value: if zero should be a solution, the answer must include zero.
ask: Which choice did you pick, and what number did you test? (expected answer: B; x = 0 gives 6 ≤ 26, which is true, and only B and C include 0)
notes.answer: B (x ≥ −5). Subtract 6: −4x ≤ 20. Divide by −4 and flip: x ≥ −5.
notes.watch: If the student chose A, have them test x = 0 in the original: it works, but 0 is not in x ≤ −5. That contradiction shows the flip was missed.

slides.title: Word Problems: Define, Write, Solve, Answer
slides.board:
1. Define the variable in words: m = number of months.
  2. Write an equation or inequality.
  3. Solve.
  4. Answer the question asked, with units. Does it make sense?
WordsMath
5 more than twice a number2n + 5
7 less than a numbern − 7
flat fee plus rate per unitfee + rate × units
at most / at least≤ / ≥

notes.say: Most GED equation questions are word problems, and many of them only ask you to choose the right equation. The four steps keep you organized. Write down what your letter means in words; that stops you from answering with the wrong quantity later. Watch "less than": seven less than a number is n minus 7, not 7 minus n, because you start with the number and take 7 away. The flat-fee-plus-rate setup is the most common one on the test: phone plans, rentals, repair bills.
ask: Translate "four less than three times a number is 20." (expected answer: 3n − 4 = 20)
Which symbol means "no more than"? (expected answer: ≤)
notes.watch: Students write 7 − n for "7 less than a number." Test with a real number: 7 less than 10 is 3, which is 10 − 7.

slides.title: An Inequality Word Problem
slides.board: A gym charges a $35 sign-up fee plus $22 per month. Ty can spend at most $200. What is the greatest number of full months he can pay for?
steps: Interpret: only full months count. 7 months costs 35 + 154 = $189 ✓; 8 months costs 35 + 176 = $211, over budget.

notes.say: The math gives m ≤ 7.5, but the question asks for full months, so we have to think about the real situation. Rounding 7.5 up to 8 would break the budget, so the answer is 7. On the GED, read the last sentence of a word problem twice: it tells you whether to round down, round up, or give the exact value.
ask: Why can't we round 7.5 up to 8? (expected answer: 8 months costs $211, which is more than $200)
Where does the $35 go in the inequality? (expected answer: added once; it is a one-time fee)
notes.watch: Watch for 200 ÷ 22 ≈ 9 (forgot the fee) and for 8 (rounded up). Both appear as wrong choices on real tests.

slides.title: Your Turn: Formulas, Inequalities, Words
slides.board:
Three minutes.

  1. Solve A = (1/2)bh for b.
  2. Solve −5x > 30.
  3. Seven less than three times a number is 26. Find the number.
  4. A phone plan costs $30 per month plus $0.05 per text. To spend at most $42 in a month, what is the greatest number of texts?

notes.say: Your turn: one formula, one inequality, and two word problems. Write the equation or inequality before you solve, and tell me your answers when the clock runs out.
ask: Read me your answers and the equation you wrote for number 3. (expected answer: b = 2A/h; x < −6; 3n − 7 = 26 so n = 11; 30 + 0.05t ≤ 42 so t ≤ 240)
notes.answer: (1) Multiply by 2: 2A = bh; divide by h: b = 2A/h   (2) Divide by −5 and flip: x < −6   (3) 3n − 7 = 26; 3n = 33; n = 11   (4) 30 + 0.05t ≤ 42; 0.05t ≤ 12; t ≤ 240, so 240 texts
notes.watch: Number 2: x > −6 means no flip. Number 3: n = 6.33 means the student wrote 3n + 7 = 26. Number 4: 840 means 42 ÷ 0.05 without subtracting the $30.

slides.title: Systems of Two Equations
slides.board:
A system is two equations that must both be true. Its solution is the (x, y) pair that works in both: where the lines cross.

  • Substitution: when one equation is already y = … or x = …
  • Elimination: when both look like Ax + By = C; add or subtract to cancel a variable.
  • Parallel lines → no solution. Same line → infinitely many.

notes.say: So far we had one equation and one unknown. A system has two unknowns and two equations, and the answer is a pair of numbers. On a graph, every point on a line makes that line's equation true, so the one point on both lines makes both equations true. Here the lines cross at (2, 3). Check it: 3 = 2 + 1, and 3 = −2 + 5. Graphing is great for seeing the idea, but algebra is faster and exact, so we will use substitution and elimination.
ask: Is (1, 2) a solution of this system? (expected answer: no; it works in y = x + 1 but −1 + 5 = 4, not 2)
notes.watch: Students often check only one equation. Make "check both" a rule: a pair that works in one equation is just a point on one line.

slides.title: Substitution
slides.board:
Solve the system:

y = 2x − 1
3x + 2y = 33
steps: The first equation says y = 2x − 1. Replace y in the second equation: 3x + 2(2x − 1) = 33
Add 2 and divide by 7: 7x = 35, so x = 5

notes.say: Substitution means "swap in an equal expression." Since y equals 2x minus 1, wherever we see y in the other equation, we put 2x minus 1 in parentheses. Now there is only one variable, and it is an ordinary multi-step equation. Do not stop at x = 5: a system needs both numbers.
ask: Why do we put 2x − 1 in parentheses? (expected answer: the 2 multiplies the whole expression)
notes.watch: Watch for 3x + 4x − 1 = 33 (the 2 did not multiply the −1). It gives x = 34/7, a messy number, which is a hint that something went wrong.

slides.title: Elimination
slides.board:
Solve the system:

3x + 4y = 2
2x − y = 5
steps: Plan: make the y-terms opposites. Multiply every term of the second equation by 4: 8x − 4y = 20
Add the equations: (3x + 4y) + (8x − 4y) = 2 + 20, so 11x = 22 and x = 2
Substitute x = 2 into 2x − y = 5: 4 − y = 5, so y = −1

notes.say: Elimination works when both equations are in the form Ax + By = C. The goal is to make one variable cancel when you add the equations. Here the y-terms are +4y and −y, so multiplying the second equation by 4 gives −4y, and they cancel. Multiply every term, including the number on the right side.
ask: What would happen if we wrote 8x − 4y = 5? (expected answer: we forgot to multiply the 5; the answer would be wrong)
notes.watch: The most common elimination error is multiplying only the left side. A second error is subtracting the equations when the terms are already opposites; opposites cancel by adding.

slides.title: A Systems Word Problem
slides.board: A school play sold 40 tickets for $395. Adult tickets cost $12 and child tickets cost $7. How many adult tickets were sold?
steps: Define: a = adult tickets, c = child tickets.
Count equation: a + c = 40. Money equation: 12a + 7c = 395
Multiply the count equation by 7: 7a + 7c = 280. Subtract it from the money equation: 5a = 115, so a = 23

notes.say: This is the classic GED system: one equation counts things, and the other adds up their value. Write both before you solve anything. Then reread the question: it asks for adult tickets, so 17 would be the right number for the wrong question. Test makers always include the other variable as a wrong choice.
ask: What does the 395 count, tickets or dollars? (expected answer: dollars, so it goes in the money equation)
notes.watch: Watch for a + c = 395 (mixing tickets and dollars). Ask the student to say the units of each equation out loud.

slides.title: Systems Together
slides.board:
Solve each system. Choose a method first.

  1. x + y = 10
    x − y = 4
  2. y = 3x
    x + y = 20
  3. 2x + y = 7
    3x − 2y = 14
steps: 1. Elimination: add the equations: 2x = 14, x = 7; then 7 + y = 10, y = 3. (7, 3)
3. Multiply the first by 2: 4x + 2y = 14. Add: 7x = 28, x = 4; 2(4) + y = 7, y = −1. (4, −1). Check: 3(4) − 2(−1) = 12 + 2 = 14 ✓

notes.say: Before solving, tell me which method you would use and why. Number 1 is ready for elimination because the y-terms are already opposites. Number 2 is ready for substitution because y is alone. Number 3 needs one multiplication first.
ask: Which method for number 2, and why? (expected answer: substitution, because y = 3x is already solved for y)
In number 3, what do you multiply by? (expected answer: multiply the first equation by 2 so the y-terms are +2y and −2y)
notes.watch: On number 3, y = 1 means a sign slip: 8 + y = 7 gives y = −1, not 1. Have the student check the pair in the second equation.

slides.title: Your Turn: Systems
slides.board:
Four minutes. Find both values and check.

  1. y = x + 4
    2x + y = 19
  2. 5x + 2y = 16
    3x − 2y = 0
  3. Two numbers have a sum of 31 and a difference of 7. Find the numbers.

notes.say: Your turn. Pick a method for each, solve for both variables, and check in both equations. For number 3, write the two equations first.
ask: Read me your answers and the two equations for number 3. (expected answer: (5, 9); (2, 3); x + y = 31 and x − y = 7, so 19 and 12)
notes.watch: Number 2: a student who subtracts the equations gets 2x + 4y = 16, with the y-terms doubled instead of canceled. Opposite terms cancel when you add. Number 3: a student who stops at 19 has found only one of the two numbers the question asks for.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Systems in Context
slides.board:
A farm stand sold 60 pounds of apples and peaches for a total of $114. Apples cost $1.50 per pound and peaches cost $2.25 per pound. How many pounds of peaches were sold?

A. 28    B. 32    C. 24    D. 50.7
steps: Eliminate A (28): that is the pounds of apples (60 − 32). The question asks for peaches.
Eliminate C (24): after multiplying a + p = 60 by 1.50 and subtracting, 0.75p = 24. 24 is the value of 0.75p; you still have to divide by 0.75.
Eliminate D (50.7): it comes from 114 ÷ 2.25, as if every pound were peaches.

notes.say: This one mixes decimals into a system, which is exactly what the calculator part of the GED likes to do. Use the calculator for the arithmetic, but write the two equations yourself. Then match your answer to the question: peaches, not apples.
ask: What are the two equations? (expected answer: a + p = 60 and 1.50a + 2.25p = 114)
Which choice is a "right number, wrong question" trap? (expected answer: A, 28, the apples)
notes.answer: B (32 pounds). a + p = 60 and 1.50a + 2.25p = 114. Multiply the first by 1.50: 1.50a + 1.50p = 90. Subtract: 0.75p = 24, so p = 32.
notes.watch: If the student is stuck setting up, ask: "What two facts do you know?" (total pounds and total dollars). Each fact is one equation.

slides.title: GED Strategy: Plug It Back In
slides.board:
1. Solve on your note board, one step per line.
  2. Plug your answer into the original equation, or into both equations of a system.
  3. Stuck? Test the answer choices in the original. The one that works is correct.
  4. Inequalities: test one value inside your answer and one outside.

Calculator: use the (−) key for negatives; check with the original numbers.

notes.say: On equation questions, the answer choices are a gift: you can always test them. Substituting a choice into the original equation tells you for certain whether it works. Even when you solve directly, the ten-second check catches the traps we saw today: the missed flip, distributing to one term, and answering for the wrong variable. On the calculator part, type the check exactly as the original is written, with parentheses.
ask: How would you check whether x > 3 is the solution of an inequality? (expected answer: test a number greater than 3, which should work, and a number less than 3, which should fail)
notes.watch: Some students check in their own simplified line instead of the original. If that line already has an error, the check passes anyway. Always check in the original.

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
• Equations: simplify, variables to one side, numbers to the other, divide, check.
  • Formulas: the same moves; treat other letters like numbers.
  • Inequalities: multiply or divide by a negative → flip. Open dot for < and >, closed for ≤ and ≥.
  • Word problems: define, write, solve, answer the question asked.
  • Systems: the pair that works in both. Substitution or elimination; check both.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice Set A → Exit Check

Next, work through the Student Lesson; each screen teaches one step and ends with a check. Then do Practice Set A. If you score under 80 percent, do Set B, which practices the same skills with different questions. Finish with the Exit Check; you pass with 6 out of 8. Next week we graph lines and work with functions, which builds directly on today.

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
This lesson teaches you to solve equations and inequalities, the most tested algebra skill on the GED math test. Work through one screen at a time. Most screens teach one step, show a worked example, and end with a check you answer before you move on. Keep paper and a pencil next to you and write every line.

By the end, you will be able to:

  • Solve one-step and multi-step equations, including equations with parentheses, fractions, and variables on both sides.
  • Solve a formula for one of its letters and use it.
  • Solve inequalities, flip the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative, and graph the answer on a number line.
  • Turn word problems into equations and inequalities and answer the question that was asked.
  • Solve a system of two equations by substitution and by elimination.

One habit runs through the whole lesson: check every answer by putting it back into the original problem.

screens.title: What It Means to Solve
screens.html:
An equation says two amounts are equal. To solve it means to find the value of the variable that makes it true. That value is the solution.

Key idea: An equation is a balance. Whatever you do to one side, do the same to the other side.

To get the variable alone, use inverse operations, which undo each other:

The equation has…Undo it by…Result
x + 6 = 10subtracting 6x = 4
x − 6 = 10adding 6x = 16
6x = 30dividing by 6x = 5
x/6 = 3multiplying by 6x = 18

steps: 9 is subtracted from x, so add 9 to both sides: x − 9 + 9 = −4 + 9.

mistakes.why: You lost the negative sign. A negative times a positive is negative: −7 × 6 = −42.
You divided by 6 instead of multiplying. n is divided by 6, so undo it by multiplying both sides by 6.

check.hint: n is divided by 6. What operation undoes division?
check.explain:
n is divided by 6, so multiply both sides by 6: n = −7 × 6 = −42.

Check: −42 ÷ 6 = −7 ✓

If you got −7/6, you divided again instead of undoing the division.

screens.title: Two-Step Equations
screens.html:
Many equations have two operations attached to the variable, like 3x + 8 = 29: x is multiplied by 3, then 8 is added.

Undo them in reverse order:

  1. First undo the addition or subtraction.
  2. Then undo the multiplication or division.

Answers can be negative numbers or fractions. 4x = 25 gives x = 25/4, which is 6 1/4 or 6.25. All three are the same value.

mistakes.why: You subtracted 9 instead of adding it (5x = 17). To undo − 9, add 9 to both sides: 5x = 35.
You stopped at 5x = 35. Divide both sides by 5 to get x alone.

check.hint: Undo the subtraction first, then undo the multiplication.
check.explain:
Add 9 to both sides: 5x = 35.

Divide both sides by 5: x = 7.

Check: 5(7) − 9 = 35 − 9 = 26 ✓

A common mistake is subtracting 9, which gives 5x = 17 and x = 3.4.

screens.title: Parentheses and Like Terms
screens.html:
When an equation has parentheses or several terms on one side, simplify each side first.

  • Distribute: multiply the number outside by every term inside. 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Combine like terms on the same side: 6x − 15 + x = 7x − 15.

Then solve the two-step equation that is left.

Watch out: 4(x − 2) is 4x − 8, not 4x − 2. The 4 multiplies both terms.

mistakes.why: You distributed the 3 to the 2x only (6x − 5). The 3 multiplies both terms: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
You subtracted 15 instead of adding it (7x = 5). To undo − 15, add 15 to both sides: 7x = 35.

check.hint: Distribute the 3 to both terms inside the parentheses, then combine the x-terms.
check.explain:
Distribute: 6x − 15 + x = 20.

Combine like terms: 7x − 15 = 20.

Add 15: 7x = 35. Divide by 7: x = 5.

Check: 3(10 − 5) + 5 = 15 + 5 = 20 ✓

If you got 25/7, you wrote 3(2x − 5) as 6x − 5.

screens.title: Variables on Both Sides
screens.html:
If both sides have a variable term, move them to one side. Subtract the smaller variable term from both sides so the coefficient stays positive.

The routine: (1) Simplify each side. (2) Variable terms to one side. (3) Numbers to the other side. (4) Divide by the coefficient. (5) Check in the original equation.

mistakes.why: You lost the negative sign. 3x = −15, and −15 ÷ 3 = −5.
You added 3 to −12 instead of subtracting it (3x = −9). To undo + 3, subtract 3 from both sides: −12 − 3 = −15.

check.hint: Subtract 5x from both sides first. Then deal with the + 3.
check.explain:
Subtract 5x from both sides: 3x + 3 = −12.

Subtract 3 from both sides: 3x = −15.

Divide by 3: x = −5.

Check: 8(−5) + 3 = −37 and 5(−5) − 12 = −37 ✓

The most common slip is −12 + 3 = −9 instead of −12 − 3 = −15.

screens.title: Equations with Fractions or Decimals
screens.html:
To clear fractions, multiply every term on both sides by the least common denominator (LCD). The fractions disappear, and you solve as usual.

Decimals: you can multiply every term by 10 or 100 to clear them, or simply work with the decimals on a calculator.

Watch out: whole-number terms get multiplied too. In x/2 + 3 = 7, multiplying by 2 gives x + 6 = 14, not x + 3 = 14.

steps: The LCD of 2 and 3 is 6. Multiply every term by 6: 3x + 2x = 60.

mistakes.why: You multiplied only the fractions by 12 and left the − 1 and + 2 alone (3x − 1 = 2x + 2). Every term gets multiplied: 3x − 12 = 2x + 24.
You subtracted 12 from 24 instead of adding (x = 24 − 12). From 3x − 12 = 2x + 24, subtract 2x and add 12: x = 36.

check.hint: The LCD of 4 and 6 is 12. Multiply every term, including the 1 and the 2, by 12.
check.explain:
Multiply every term by 12: 3x − 12 = 2x + 24.

Subtract 2x: x − 12 = 24.

Add 12: x = 36.

Check: 36/4 − 1 = 9 − 1 = 8 and 36/6 + 2 = 6 + 2 = 8 ✓

screens.title: No Solution or Infinitely Many
screens.html:
Sometimes the variable terms cancel out completely. Read what is left:

  • A false statement, like 8 = 5: no number works. The equation has no solution.
  • A true statement, like 6 = 6: every number works. The equation has infinitely many solutions.
  • If you end with x = a number (even x = 0), there is exactly one solution.

example.answer: Infinitely many solutions. Both sides are the same expression.

check.prompt:
Choose the phrase that describes each equation.

2(x − 3) = 2x − 5 has {{0}}.

4x + 8 = 4(x + 2) has {{1}}.

5x − 1 = 3x − 1 has {{2}}.

why: Distributing gives 2x − 6 = 2x − 5. The x-terms cancel and leave −6 = −5, which is false, so no value of x works.
The x-terms cancel, but what is left, −6 = −5, is false. Infinitely many solutions needs a true statement such as 5 = 5.
Distributing the right side gives 4x + 8, the same as the left side. Every value of x works, not just one.
The x-terms cancel and leave 8 = 8, which is true. A true statement means every number works, not that none do.
Subtracting 3x gives 2x − 1 = −1, so 2x = 0 and x = 0. Zero is a real solution; the variable did not cancel.
The x-terms do not cancel here because 5x and 3x are different. The equation has the single solution x = 0.

check.hint: Simplify both sides. Do the x-terms cancel? If they do, is what is left true or false?
check.explain:
First: 2x − 6 = 2x − 5 → −6 = −5, false → no solution.

Second: 4x + 8 = 4x + 8 → 8 = 8, true → infinitely many solutions.

Third: 2x − 1 = −1 → 2x = 0 → x = 0, so exactly one solution. A solution of 0 is still a solution.

screens.title: Solving a Formula for a Letter
screens.html:
A literal equation has two or more letters, like a formula. To "solve for w" means to get w alone on one side.

Use exactly the same moves you use with numbers. Treat every other letter as if it were a number. Ask: What is being done to the letter I want? Then undo it.

FormulaSolved for…Move
d = rtt = d/rdivide by r
A = (1/2)bhh = 2A/bmultiply by 2, divide by b
y = mx + bx = (y − b)/msubtract b, divide by m

steps: Multiply both sides by 2 to undo the 1/2: 2A = bh.
h is multiplied by b, so divide both sides by b: 2A/b = h.

check.prompt: The volume of a box is V = lwh. Which equation is solved for w?
why: You subtracted lh, but w is multiplied by l and h, not added to them. Undo multiplication by dividing both sides by lh.
You divided in the wrong order and turned the fraction upside down. From V = lwh, divide both sides by lh: V/(lh) = w, with V on top.
You multiplied by l and h instead of dividing. Multiplying does not undo multiplication; dividing both sides by lh does.
check.hint: In lwh, w is multiplied by l and h. What undoes multiplication?
check.explain:
In V = lwh, w is multiplied by l and by h.

Divide both sides by lh: V/(lh) = w.

So w = V/(lh).

Check with numbers: a box 2 by 3 by 4 has V = 24. V/(lh) = 24/(2 × 4) = 3 = w ✓. The tempting choice lh/V gives 8/24, which is not 3.

screens.title: Solve a Formula, Then Use It
screens.html:
Many GED questions give you a formula and ask for a letter that is not alone. You have two options:

  1. Solve the formula for that letter, then substitute the numbers.
  2. Substitute the numbers first, then solve the equation.

Both give the same answer. Solving first is handy when you must use the formula many times.

example.prompt: The perimeter of a rectangle is P = 2l + 2w. Find w when P = 46 feet and l = 14 feet.
steps: Solve for w: P − 2l = 2w, so w = (P − 2l)/2.

check.prompt:
Simple interest is I = Prt, where P is the principal, r is the yearly rate as a decimal, and t is the time in years.

A $2,000 loan earns $240 in interest over 3 years. Solve for r and find the rate. Enter r as a decimal.

mistakes.why: You divided 240 by 2,000 and left out the 3 years. r is multiplied by both P and t, so divide by Pt = 2,000 × 3 = 6,000.
You turned the fraction upside down (6,000 ÷ 240). Solving I = Prt for r gives r = I/(Pt), with the interest on top.

check.hint: r is multiplied by P and by t. Divide both sides by Pt.
check.explain:
Solve for r: r = I/(Pt).

Substitute: r = 240/(2,000 × 3) = 240/6,000 = 0.04, which is a 4% rate.

Check: 2,000 × 0.04 × 3 = 240 ✓

If you got 0.12, you divided by 2,000 only; that is the interest rate for all 3 years together, not per year.

screens.title: Inequalities and Their Graphs
screens.html:
An inequality compares two amounts that may not be equal. Its solution is usually a whole range of numbers, which you show on a number line.

SymbolMeaningDot
<is less thanopen (not included)
>is greater thanopen (not included)
≤is less than or equal toclosed (included)

screens.title: Solving Inequalities: The Flip Rule
screens.html:
Solve an inequality with the same steps as an equation, with one extra rule:

The flip rule: when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.

Why? 2 < 5 is true. Multiply both sides by −1: −2 and −5. Now −2 is the larger number, so the sign must turn around: −2 > −5.

Only flip for multiplying or dividing by a negative. In 3x < −12, you divide by positive 3, so x < −4 with no flip.

steps: Divide by −4 and flip the sign: x < −3.
Graph: open dot at −3, shaded left. Check x = −4: −4(−4) + 3 = 19, and 19 > 15 ✓

check.prompt:
What is the greatest integer that is a solution of the inequality below?

10 − 3x ≥ 31

mistakes.why: You lost the negative sign: 21 ÷ (−3) = −7. The solution is x ≤ −7, so the greatest integer is −7.
You added 10 instead of subtracting it (−3x ≥ 41, so x ≤ −13.67). Subtract 10 from both sides: −3x ≥ 21.
You left out −7 itself. The sign ≤ includes −7: 10 − 3(−7) = 31, and 31 ≥ 31 is true.

check.hint: Subtract 10 first. You will divide by a negative number, so watch the sign.
check.explain:
Subtract 10 from both sides: −3x ≥ 21.

Divide by −3 and flip the sign: x ≤ −7.

The solutions are −7 and every number less than −7, so the greatest integer is −7.

Check: 10 − 3(−7) = 10 + 21 = 31, and 31 ≥ 31 ✓. Try −6: 10 + 18 = 28, and 28 ≥ 31 is false, so nothing greater than −7 works.

screens.title: From Words to Equations
screens.html:
Translate a sentence into math one piece at a time.

WordsMath
twice a number2n
5 more than a numbern + 5
7 less than a numbern − 7 (not 7 − n)
the sum of a number and 4, times 33(n + 4)
is, equals, the result is=
at most / no more than≤
at least / no less than≥

Test "less than" with real numbers: 7 less than 10 is 3, which is 10 − 7.

example.prompt: Five more than twice a number is 31. Find the number.
steps: Twice a number: 2n. Five more than that: 2n + 5. Is 31: 2n + 5 = 31.

check.prompt: Eight less than three times a number, n, is 22. Which equation can be used to find n?
why: You reversed the order. "Eight less than" a quantity means start with the quantity and take 8 away: 3n − 8.
This subtracts 8 from n before tripling. The sentence triples the number first, then takes away 8: 3n − 8.
"Less than" means subtract, not add. Eight less than 3n is 3n − 8.
check.hint: Write "three times a number" first. Then take 8 away from it.
check.explain:
"Three times a number" is 3n.

"Eight less than" that amount means subtract 8 from it: 3n − 8.

"Is 22" means = 22. The equation is 3n − 8 = 22 (so n = 10).

The tempting choice 8 − 3n = 22 reverses the order. Test with numbers: 8 less than 30 is 22, which is 30 − 8.

screens.title: Solving Equation Word Problems
screens.html:
Use four steps on every word problem:

  1. Define the variable in words: h = number of hours.
  2. Write an equation.
  3. Solve it.
  4. Answer the question that was asked, with units, and check that it makes sense.

The most common GED setup is a flat fee plus a rate per unit: total = fee + rate × units. The fee is added once; the rate is multiplied by the number of units.

example.prompt: A plumber charges $65 for a house call plus $48 per hour. The bill was $257. How many hours did the plumber work?

check.prompt: A van rental costs $40 plus $0.25 per mile. Lena's bill was $97.50. How many miles did she drive?

mistakes.why: You divided the whole bill by 0.25 ($97.50 ÷ 0.25) and forgot the $40 fee. Subtract the fee first: $97.50 − $40 = $57.50.
You added the $40 fee instead of subtracting it ($137.50 ÷ 0.25). The fee is part of the bill, so take it away: $57.50 ÷ 0.25 = 230.

check.hint: Write fee + rate × miles = bill. Subtract the fee before you divide.
check.explain:
Let m = miles. 40 + 0.25m = 97.50.

Subtract 40: 0.25m = 57.50.

Divide by 0.25: m = 230 miles.

Check: 40 + 0.25(230) = 40 + 57.50 = $97.50 ✓

Dividing $97.50 by 0.25 without subtracting the fee gives 390, the most common wrong answer.

screens.title: Inequality Word Problems
screens.html:
Words like at most, no more than, at least, and a minimum of signal an inequality.

After you solve, think about the situation. If the answer must be a whole number (people, months, tickets):

  • "At most" problems usually round down, so you stay under the limit.
  • "At least" problems usually round up, so you reach the goal.

Always test your whole number in the original situation.

example.prompt: A gym charges a $35 sign-up fee plus $22 per month. Ty can spend at most $200. What is the greatest number of full months he can pay for?
steps: Only full months count. 7 months costs $189; 8 months costs $211, which is over budget.

check.prompt: Rosa needs at least $1,000 for a security deposit. She has $280 saved and adds $65 each week. What is the fewest whole weeks she must save to have at least $1,000?

mistakes.why: You rounded 11.08 down. After 11 weeks Rosa has 280 + 715 = $995, which is short of $1,000. "At least" means round up: 12 weeks.
You divided $1,000 by $65 and left out the $280 she already has. Subtract it first: $1,000 − $280 = $720.

check.hint: Write savings + 65 × weeks ≥ 1,000. After you divide, decide whether to round up or down.
check.explain:
Let w = weeks. 280 + 65w ≥ 1,000.

Subtract 280: 65w ≥ 720.

Divide by 65: w ≥ 11.08…

She needs a whole number of weeks that is at least 11.08, so 12 weeks.

Check: after 11 weeks, 280 + 715 = $995 (not enough); after 12 weeks, 280 + 780 = $1,060 ✓

screens.title: Systems: What a Solution Means
screens.html:
A system of equations is two equations that must be true at the same time. Its solution is an ordered pair (x, y) that works in both equations.

On a graph, each equation is a line. Every point on a line makes that equation true, so the point where the two lines cross makes both true.

In the graph below, y = 2x − 1 and y = −x + 5 cross at (2, 3). Check: 2(2) − 1 = 3 ✓ and −2 + 5 = 3 ✓.

  • Parallel lines never cross: no solution.
  • The same line twice: infinitely many solutions.

check.prompt: The graph shows the lines y = x + 3 and y = −2x + 6. Click the point that is the solution of the system.
check.why: The most common mistake is clicking where one line crosses an axis, such as (0, 3) or (0, 6). Those points are on only one line. The solution is where the two lines cross each other: (1, 4).
check.hint: Find the one point that is on both lines.
check.explain:
The lines cross at (1, 4).

Check in both equations: 1 + 3 = 4 ✓ and −2(1) + 6 = 4 ✓.

Algebra agrees: x + 3 = −2x + 6 gives 3x = 3, so x = 1 and y = 4.

screens.title: Solving Systems by Substitution
screens.html:
Substitution works well when one equation already says y = … or x = ….

  1. Replace that variable in the other equation with its expression, in parentheses.
  2. Solve the one-variable equation.
  3. Put that value back in to find the other variable.
  4. Check the pair in both equations.

example.prompt: Solve y = x + 4 and x + y = 12.

check.prompt:
Solve the system below. What is the value of y?

y = 2x + 3
3x + y = 23

mistakes.why: That is the value of x. Put x = 4 back into y = 2x + 3 to find y: 2(4) + 3 = 11.
You added 3 to 23 instead of subtracting it (5x = 26, so x = 5.2). From 5x + 3 = 23, subtract 3: 5x = 20.

check.hint: Replace y in the second equation with (2x + 3). Solve for x, then find y.
check.explain:
Substitute: 3x + (2x + 3) = 23.

Combine: 5x + 3 = 23, so 5x = 20 and x = 4.

Find y: y = 2(4) + 3 = 11.

Check: 3(4) + 11 = 23 ✓

Be careful to answer with y. The value 4 is x.

screens.title: Solving Systems by Elimination
screens.html:
Elimination works well when both equations look like Ax + By = C.

  1. Make one variable's terms opposites, such as +2y and −2y. Multiply an equation by a number if needed; multiply every term, including the constant.
  2. Add the equations. That variable cancels.
  3. Solve, then substitute to find the other variable.
  4. Check in both equations.

steps: The y-terms are already opposites (+3y and −3y). Add the equations: 6x = 18, so x = 3.
Substitute into the first: 2(3) + 3y = 12, so 3y = 6 and y = 2.

check.prompt:
Solve the system below. What is the value of x?

2x + y = 11
3x − 2y = 6

mistakes.why: You multiplied only the left side of 2x + y = 11 by 2 and kept 11 (4x + 2y = 11). Multiply every term: 4x + 2y = 22.
That is the value of y. The question asks for x, which is 4.

check.hint: Multiply the first equation by 2 so the y-terms become +2y and −2y. Then add.
check.explain:
Multiply every term of the first equation by 2: 4x + 2y = 22.

Add it to the second: (4x + 2y) + (3x − 2y) = 22 + 6, so 7x = 28 and x = 4.

Find y: 2(4) + y = 11, so y = 3.

Check: 3(4) − 2(3) = 12 − 6 = 6 ✓

screens.title: Systems Word Problems
screens.html:
When a word problem has two unknowns, write two equations. Usually:

  • One equation counts the items: a + c = total number.
  • The other adds up their value: price × a + price × c = total dollars.

Solve, then reread the question. Test makers always offer the other variable as a wrong answer.

example.prompt: A cashier has 30 bills, all $5 and $10 bills, worth $215. How many $10 bills are there?
steps: Let f = $5 bills and t = $10 bills. Count: f + t = 30. Value: 5f + 10t = 215.
Multiply the count equation by 5: 5f + 5t = 150. Subtract it from the value equation: 5t = 65, so t = 13.

check.prompt: Jordan bought 12 plants for his porch. Herbs cost $4 each and flowers cost $7 each. He spent $63. How many flowers did he buy?

mistakes.why: That is the number of herbs (12 − 5). The question asks for flowers.
You stopped at 3f = 15. Divide by 3: f = 5.

check.hint: Write one equation for the number of plants and one for the money. Multiply the plant equation by 4, then subtract.
check.explain:
Let h = herbs and f = flowers. h + f = 12 and 4h + 7f = 63.

Multiply the first by 4: 4h + 4f = 48.

Subtract from the money equation: 3f = 15, so f = 5 flowers.

Then h = 7. Check: 7 + 5 = 12 ✓ and 4(7) + 7(5) = 28 + 35 = 63 ✓

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• To solve, keep the balance: do the same thing to both sides, using inverse operations.
  • Routine: simplify each side, variables to one side, numbers to the other, divide, check in the original.
  • Clear fractions by multiplying every term by the LCD.
  • If the variables cancel: a false statement means no solution; a true statement means infinitely many.
  • Solve a formula for a letter with the same moves; treat the other letters like numbers.
  • Inequalities: multiply or divide by a negative → flip the sign. Open dot for < and >; closed dot for ≤ and ≥.
  • Word problems: define, write, solve, answer the question asked. "At most" is ≤; "at least" is ≥. Round to fit the situation.
  • A system's solution is the pair that works in both equations, where the lines cross. Use substitution when a variable is alone, elimination when both are in Ax + By = C form.

Next: Practice Set A. If you score under 80%, practice the same skills again with Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

An open dot at −3, shaded to the right

The symbol ≥ means “greater than or equal to,” so −3 itself is part of the solution. That calls for a closed (filled) dot.

Numbers greater than −3 (such as −2, 0, and 5) lie to the right of −3, so shade to the right.

An open dot would be used for x > −3, where −3 is not included. Shading to the left would show x ≤ −3.

items.prompt: Six less than four times a number is 30. What is the number?

mistakes.why: You wrote 4n + 6 = 30. "Six less than" means subtract 6: 4n − 6 = 30.

"Four times a number" is 4n. "Six less than" that is 4n − 6. "Is 30" means = 30.

4n − 6 = 30. Add 6: 4n = 36. Divide by 4: n = 9.

Check: 4(9) − 6 = 36 − 6 = 30 ✓

The most common error is 4n + 6 = 30, which gives 6. "Less than" means subtract.

items.prompt:

3(x + 4) = 27

You added 12 to 27 instead of subtracting it (3x = 39). To undo + 12, subtract 12: 3x = 15.

items.hint: Distribute the 3 to both terms in the parentheses, or divide both sides by 3 first.
items.explain:
Distribute: 3x + 12 = 27.

Subtract 12: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5.

Another way: divide both sides by 3 first: x + 4 = 9, so x = 5.

Check: 3(5 + 4) = 3(9) = 27 ✓

items.prompt:
What is the value of x in the equation below?

You subtracted 8 from 10 instead of adding (2x = 2). From 2x − 8 = 10, add 8 to both sides: 2x = 18.
You added 4x to both sides instead of subtracting it (10x − 8 = 10). To move 4x off the right side, subtract it: 2x − 8 = 10.
items.hint: Distribute the 2 to both terms inside the parentheses. Then get all the x-terms on one side.
items.explain:
Distribute: 2(3x) − 2(4) = 6x − 8, so 6x − 8 = 4x + 10

Subtract 4x from both sides: 2x − 8 = 10

Add 8 to both sides: 2x = 18

Divide by 2: x = 9

Check: 2(3 × 9 − 4) = 2(23) = 46 and 4(9) + 10 = 46. Correct.

items.prompt:
Kendra is solving the equation 2x + 3y = 12 for y. Choose the correct option for each blank.

Step 1: Subtract {{0}} from both sides to get 3y = 12 − 2x.

Step 2: Divide both sides by {{1}}.

Result: y = {{2}}

why: Subtracting 3y would remove the term you are trying to keep. To isolate the y-term, remove the x-term, 2x.
Subtracting 12 does not give 3y = 12 − 2x. The x-term, 2x, is what has to move to the other side.
Subtracting just the number 2 leaves the x behind. Subtract the whole term 2x.
y is multiplied by 3, not 2. The 2 belongs to the x-term. Divide by the coefficient of y, which is 3.

Substitute x = 4 into the first equation: 3(4) + 2y = 4, so 12 + 2y = 4, 2y = −8, and y = −4

Solution: (4, −4)

Check in the second equation: 5(4) − 4(−4) = 20 + 16 = 36. Correct.

The pair (8, −10) works in the first equation (24 − 20 = 4) but not the second (40 + 40 = 80), which is why a solution must be checked in both equations. (−4, 4) reverses the coordinates, and (4, 4) has a sign error in y.

items.prompt: A community theater sold 150 tickets for one performance and collected $1,620. Adult tickets cost $14 each and student tickets cost $8 each. How many student tickets were sold?

mistakes.why: That is the number of adult tickets. The question asks for student tickets: 150 − 70 = 80.
You stopped at 6a = 420. Divide by 6 to get a = 70 adult tickets, then subtract from 150 to get the student tickets.

items.hint: Write one equation for the number of tickets and one for the money. Multiply the ticket equation by 8 so you can eliminate s.
items.explain:
Let a = adult tickets and s = student tickets.

Tickets: a + s = 150

Money: 14a + 8s = 1,620

Multiply the ticket equation by 8: 8a + 8s = 1,200

Subtract it from the money equation: (14a + 8s) − (8a + 8s) = 1,620 − 1,200, so 6a = 420 and a = 70

Then s = 150 − 70 = 80 student tickets.

Check: 70 + 80 = 150, and 14(70) + 8(80) = 980 + 640 = 1,620. Correct.

Be careful: 70 is the number of adult tickets. The question asks for student tickets.

items.prompt: The volume of a cylinder is V = πr2h. A cylindrical water tank holds 1,570 cubic feet and has a radius of 5 feet. Use 3.14 for π. Solve the formula for h and find the height of the tank, in feet.

mistakes.why: You used r instead of r<sup>2</sup> (3.14 × 5 = 15.7). The radius is squared: 3.14 × 25 = 78.5.
You doubled the radius instead of squaring it (3.14 × 10 = 31.4). r<sup>2</sup> means 5 × 5 = 25, not 5 × 2.

items.hint: h is multiplied by π and by r<sup>2</sup>. Divide both sides by πr<sup>2</sup>.
items.explain:
Solve for h: h = V/(πr2).

πr2 = 3.14 × 52 = 3.14 × 25 = 78.5.

h = 1,570 ÷ 78.5 = 20 feet.

Check: 3.14 × 25 × 20 = 1,570 ✓

Forgetting to square the radius gives 100, the most common wrong answer.

items.prompt:
Solve for x.

4(2x − 3) − 5x = 2x + 9

mistakes.why: You distributed the 4 to the 2x only (8x − 3). The 4 multiplies both terms: 4(2x − 3) = 8x − 12.
You subtracted 12 from 9 instead of adding (x = 9 − 12). From x − 12 = 9, add 12 to both sides: x = 21.

items.hint: Distribute, combine like terms on the left, then get the x-terms on one side.
items.explain:
Distribute: 8x − 12 − 5x = 2x + 9.

Combine like terms: 3x − 12 = 2x + 9.

Subtract 2x: x − 12 = 9. Add 12: x = 21.

Check: 4(42 − 3) − 105 = 156 − 105 = 51 and 2(21) + 9 = 51 ✓

If you got 12, you wrote 4(2x − 3) as 8x − 3.

items.prompt: The perimeter of a rectangle is P = 2(l + w). Which equation is solved for l?
why: You subtracted w before dividing by 2, but w is inside the parentheses that are multiplied by 2. Divide by 2 first: P/2 = l + w, then subtract w.
You added w instead of subtracting it. From P/2 = l + w, subtract w from both sides: l = P/2 − w.
You divided only the w by 2. Dividing both sides by 2 divides P, not w: P/2 = l + w.
items.hint: Divide both sides by 2 first. Then undo the + w.
items.explain:
Divide both sides by 2: P/2 = l + w.

Subtract w from both sides: l = P/2 − w.

Check with numbers: a 7-by-3 rectangle has P = 20. P/2 − w = 10 − 3 = 7 = l ✓. The choice (P − w)/2 gives (20 − 3)/2 = 8.5, which is not 7.

items.prompt:
Solve −2x + 7 > 15 and describe its graph. Choose the correct option for each blank.

Solution: x {{0}} {{1}}

Graph: {{2}} dot at the boundary, shaded to the {{3}}.

why: You did not flip the sign. Dividing −2x > 8 by −2 reverses > to <.
The original sign is >, so the endpoint is not included. Flipping > gives <, not ≤.
You did not flip the sign, and you added "or equal to." Dividing by −2 turns > into <.
Check the sign: 8 ÷ (−2) = −4, not 4.
You added 7 instead of subtracting it (−2x > 22). Subtract 7 from both sides: −2x > 8.
The sign < does not include −4 itself, so the dot is open. Closed dots are for ≤ and ≥.
Solutions of x < −4 are numbers less than −4, such as −5 and −10, which lie to the left.

items.hint: Subtract 7, then divide by −2. What happens to the sign when you divide by a negative?
items.explain:
Subtract 7 from both sides: −2x > 8.

Divide by −2 and flip the sign: x < −4.

Graph: an open dot at −4 (−4 is not included), shaded to the left.

Check x = −5: −2(−5) + 7 = 17, and 17 > 15 ✓. Check x = 0: 7 > 15 is false ✓.

The most common mistake is x > −4, from forgetting to flip.

items.prompt: A delivery van can carry at most 1,500 pounds. The driver weighs 190 pounds, and each box weighs 45 pounds. What is the greatest number of boxes the van can carry with the driver on board?

mistakes.why: You rounded 29.1 up. Thirty boxes plus the driver weigh 190 + 1,350 = 1,540 pounds, which is over the limit. With "at most," round down.
You divided 1,500 by 45 and left out the driver. Subtract the driver's weight first: 1,500 − 190 = 1,310.
You added the driver's weight to 1,500 instead of subtracting it (1,690 ÷ 45). The driver uses up part of the 1,500 pounds.

items.hint: Write driver + 45 × boxes ≤ 1,500. Subtract before you divide, then round to fit the situation.
items.explain:
Let b = boxes. 190 + 45b ≤ 1,500.

Subtract 190: 45b ≤ 1,310. Divide by 45: b ≤ 29.1…

Only whole boxes count, so the greatest number is 29.

Check: 190 + 45(29) = 190 + 1,305 = 1,495 ≤ 1,500 ✓; 30 boxes would make 1,540 pounds.

items.prompt: A plumber charges a $55 service fee plus $40 per hour. A customer's bill was $235. Which equation can be used to find h, the number of hours the plumber worked?
why: This switches the fee and the rate. The $55 fee is charged once; the $40 is charged for each hour, so it multiplies h.
This charges the $55 fee every hour. The fee is charged once, so only the $40 rate multiplies h.
The fee is added to the hourly charges, not subtracted. The bill is fee plus hourly charges: 55 + 40h.
items.hint: Which amount is charged once, and which is charged for each hour?
items.explain:
The bill is the one-time fee plus the hourly rate times the hours: fee + rate × hours = bill.

55 + 40h = 235. (Solving: 40h = 180, so h = 4.5 hours.)

The tempting choice 40 + 55h = 235 swaps the fee and the rate.

items.prompt: The graph shows the lines y = 2x − 3 and y = −x + 6. Click the point that is the solution of the system.
items.why: The most common mistake is clicking a y-intercept, (0, −3) or (0, 6). Each of those points is on only one line. The solution is where the lines cross: (3, 3).
items.explain:
The lines cross at (3, 3).

Check: 2(3) − 3 = 3 ✓ and −3 + 6 = 3 ✓.

Algebra agrees: 2x − 3 = −x + 6, so 3x = 9, x = 3, and y = 3.

items.prompt:
Solve the system of equations below. What is the value of y?

3x + 4y = 10
5x − 2y = 34

mistakes.why: That is the value of x. Substitute x = 6 into 3x + 4y = 10: 18 + 4y = 10, so y = −2.
Check the sign: 18 + 4y = 10 gives 4y = −8, so y = −2.

items.hint: Multiply the second equation by 2 so the y-terms become +4y and −4y.
items.explain:
Multiply the second equation by 2: 10x − 4y = 68.

Add it to the first: 13x = 78, so x = 6.

Substitute: 3(6) + 4y = 10, so 4y = −8 and y = −2.

Check the second equation: 5(6) − 2(−2) = 30 + 4 = 34 ✓

items.prompt: A school office bought 25 items for $119. Notebooks cost $3 each and binders cost $7 each. How many binders did the office buy?
why: 14 is the number of notebooks (25 − 11). The question asks for binders.
You divided $119 by $7, as if every item were a binder. The office bought two kinds of items; use both equations.
You stopped at 4b = 44. Divide by 4: b = 11.
items.hint: Write one equation for the number of items and one for the cost. Multiply the count equation by 3 and subtract.
items.explain:
Let n = notebooks and b = binders. n + b = 25 and 3n + 7b = 119.

Multiply the first by 3: 3n + 3b = 75. Subtract from the cost equation: 4b = 44, so b = 11.

Then n = 14. Check: 14 + 11 = 25 ✓ and 3(14) + 7(11) = 42 + 77 = 119 ✓

14 is the number of notebooks, the most tempting wrong answer.

items.prompt:
Solve for x.

6(x + 2) − 4x = 5x − 9

mistakes.why: You distributed the 6 to the x only (6x + 2). The 6 multiplies both terms: 6(x + 2) = 6x + 12.
You combined 12 and −9 as 3 instead of 21. From 2x + 12 = 5x − 9, add 9 to both sides: 2x + 21 = 5x, so 21 = 3x.

items.hint: Distribute and combine like terms on the left. Then subtract the smaller x-term from both sides.
items.explain:
Distribute: 6x + 12 − 4x = 5x − 9.

Combine like terms: 2x + 12 = 5x − 9.

Subtract 2x: 12 = 3x − 9. Add 9: 21 = 3x. Divide by 3: x = 7.

Check: 6(9) − 28 = 54 − 28 = 26 and 5(7) − 9 = 26 ✓

items.prompt: The equation of a line is y = mx + b. Which equation is solved for x?
why: You divided before subtracting, so b was not divided by m. Undo the + b first: y − b = mx, then divide the whole side by m.
You added b instead of subtracting it. To undo + b, subtract b from both sides: y − b = mx.
You multiplied by m instead of dividing. x is multiplied by m, so divide both sides by m.
items.hint: Undo the + b first. Then undo the multiplication by m.
items.explain:
Subtract b from both sides: y − b = mx.

Divide both sides by m: x = (y − b)/m.

Check with numbers: if m = 2, b = 1, and x = 3, then y = 7. (y − b)/m = 6/2 = 3 ✓. The choice y/m − b gives 3.5 − 1 = 2.5, which is not 3.

items.prompt:
Solve 3 − 4x ≤ 23 and describe its graph. Choose the correct option for each blank.

Solution: x {{0}} {{1}}

Graph: {{2}} dot at the boundary, shaded to the {{3}}.

why: You did not flip the sign, and you dropped "or equal to." Dividing by −4 turns ≤ into ≥.
You flipped the sign but dropped "or equal to." The original ≤ includes the endpoint, so the flipped sign is ≥.
You did not flip the sign. Dividing −4x ≤ 20 by −4 reverses ≤ to ≥.
Check the sign: 20 ÷ (−4) = −5, not 5.
You added 3 instead of subtracting it (−4x ≤ 26). Subtract 3 from both sides: −4x ≤ 20.
The sign ≥ includes −5 itself, so the dot is closed. Open dots are for < and >.
Solutions of x ≥ −5 are numbers greater than −5, such as 0 and 3, which lie to the right.

items.hint: Subtract 3, then divide by −4. Does the sign flip? Is the endpoint included?
items.explain:
Subtract 3 from both sides: −4x ≤ 20.

Divide by −4 and flip the sign: x ≥ −5.

Graph: a closed dot at −5 (−5 is included), shaded to the right.

Check x = 0: 3 ≤ 23 ✓. Check x = −6: 3 + 24 = 27, and 27 ≤ 23 is false ✓.

items.prompt: A banquet hall charges a $450 room fee plus $28 per guest. The Ortiz family can spend at most $2,000. What is the greatest number of guests they can invite?

mistakes.why: You rounded 55.4 up. Fifty-six guests would cost 450 + 1,568 = $2,018, which is over the budget. With "at most," round down.
You divided $2,000 by $28 and left out the $450 room fee. Subtract the fee first: $2,000 − $450 = $1,550.
You added the fee to the budget instead of subtracting it ($2,450 ÷ 28). The fee uses up part of the $2,000.

items.hint: Write fee + 28 × guests ≤ 2,000. Subtract the fee before you divide, then round to fit the situation.
items.explain:
Let g = guests. 450 + 28g ≤ 2,000.

Subtract 450: 28g ≤ 1,550. Divide by 28: g ≤ 55.3…

Only whole guests count, so the greatest number is 55.

Check: 450 + 28(55) = 450 + 1,540 = $1,990 ✓; 56 guests would cost $2,018.

items.prompt: A kayak rental costs $12 for a life jacket and paddle plus $9 per hour. Dev paid $57. Which equation can be used to find h, the number of hours he rented the kayak?
why: This switches the one-time charge and the rate. The $9 is charged for each hour, so it multiplies h; the $12 is charged once.
This charges the $12 every hour. The $12 is a one-time charge, so only the $9 rate multiplies h.
The $12 is added to the hourly charges, not subtracted. Total = 12 + 9h.
items.hint: Which amount is charged once, and which is charged for each hour?
items.explain:
Total cost = one-time charge + hourly rate × hours.

12 + 9h = 57. (Solving: 9h = 45, so h = 5 hours.)

The tempting choice 9 + 12h = 57 swaps the one-time charge and the rate.

items.prompt: The graph shows the lines y = x + 2 and y = −2x + 8. Click the point that is the solution of the system.
items.why: The most common mistake is clicking a y-intercept, (0, 2) or (0, 8). Each of those points is on only one line. The solution is where the lines cross: (2, 4).
items.explain:
The lines cross at (2, 4).

Check: 2 + 2 = 4 ✓ and −2(2) + 8 = 4 ✓.

Algebra agrees: x + 2 = −2x + 8, so 3x = 6, x = 2, and y = 4.

items.prompt:
Solve the system of equations below. What is the value of y?

2x + 3y = −1
5x + 2y = 14

mistakes.why: That is the value of x. Substitute x = 4 into 2x + 3y = −1: 8 + 3y = −1, so y = −3.
Check the sign: 8 + 3y = −1 gives 3y = −9, so y = −3.

items.hint: Multiply the first equation by 2 and the second by 3 so both y-terms become 6y. Then subtract.
items.explain:
Multiply the first equation by 2: 4x + 6y = −2.

Multiply the second equation by 3: 15x + 6y = 42.

Subtract the first from the second: 11x = 44, so x = 4.

Substitute: 2(4) + 3y = −1, so 3y = −9 and y = −3.

Check the second equation: 5(4) + 2(−3) = 20 − 6 = 14 ✓

items.prompt: A fruit stand sold 40 baskets of berries, some small and some large. Small baskets cost $6 and large baskets cost $10. The stand took in $328. How many large baskets were sold?
why: 18 is the number of small baskets (40 − 22). The question asks for large baskets.
You divided $328 by $10, as if every basket were large. Use both equations: the count and the money.
You stopped at 4l = 88. Divide by 4: l = 22.
items.hint: Write one equation for the number of baskets and one for the money. Multiply the count equation by 6 and subtract.
items.explain:
Let s = small and l = large. s + l = 40 and 6s + 10l = 328.

Multiply the first by 6: 6s + 6l = 240. Subtract from the money equation: 4l = 88, so l = 22.

Then s = 18. Check: 18 + 22 = 40 ✓ and 6(18) + 10(22) = 108 + 220 = 328 ✓

18 is the number of small baskets, the most tempting wrong answer.

vocab.def: A math sentence that says two expressions are equal.
A letter that stands for an unknown number.
A value that makes an equation or inequality true.
Operations that undo each other, such as addition and subtraction, or multiplication and division.
The number multiplied by a variable.
A number with no variable attached.
Terms with the same variable raised to the same power; they can be combined.
Multiplying a number by each term inside parentheses.
An equation with two or more letters, such as a formula, that you solve for one of the letters.
vocab.example: d = rt solved for t is t = d/r.

vocab.def: A math sentence that compares two amounts using <, >, ≤, or ≥.
On a number-line graph, an open dot means the endpoint is not included (<, >); a closed dot means it is included (≤, ≥).
vocab.example: x ≤ 2 has a closed dot at 2.

vocab.def: Two or more equations that must be true at the same time.
Solving a system by replacing one variable with an equal expression from the other equation.
vocab.example: If y = 2x, replace y with 2x in x + y = 9.

vocab.def: Solving a system by adding or subtracting the equations so one variable cancels out.
vocab.example: Adding x + y = 10 and x − y = 4 gives 2x = 14.

vocab.def: When the variable cancels out of an equation: a false statement that remains (such as 8 = 5) means no number works; a true statement (such as 6 = 6) means every number works.
vocab.example: 2(x + 4) = 2x + 5 has no solution; 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6 has infinitely many.

notes:
Week 8 Study Sheet: Equations and Inequalities

Solving Linear Equations

  1. Simplify each side (distribute, combine like terms).
  2. Variable terms to one side.
  3. Numbers to the other side.
  4. Divide by the coefficient.
  5. Check in the original equation.

4(x − 2) = 2x + 10 → 4x − 8 = 2x + 10 → 2x = 18 → x = 9

Fractions: multiply every term by the LCD. x/2 + x/3 = 10 → 3x + 2x = 60 → x = 12

Variables cancel: false (8 = 5) → no solution; true (6 = 6) → infinitely many.

Formulas (Literal Equations)

Same moves; treat the other letters like numbers.

  • d = rt → t = d/r
  • P = 2l + 2w → w = (P − 2l)/2
  • A = (1/2)bh → h = 2A/b
  • y = mx + b → x = (y − b)/m
  • I = Prt → r = I/(Pt)
  • F = 1.8C + 32 → C = (F − 32)/1.8

Inequalities

SymbolWordsDot
<less thanopen
>greater thanopen
≤at most / no more thanclosed
≥at least / no less thanclosed

Flip rule: multiply or divide by a negative → reverse the sign.

7 − 3x ≥ 19 → −3x ≥ 12 → x ≤ −4 (closed dot at −4, shade left)

With x on the left, the symbol points the way to shade. Test one value inside and one outside.

Systems of Two Equations

Solution = the (x, y) pair that works in both = where the lines cross. Parallel lines: no solution; same line: infinitely many.

Substitution: y = x + 4 and x + y = 12 → x + (x + 4) = 12 → x = 4, y = 8

Elimination: 2x + 3y = 12 and 4x − 3y = 6 → add: 6x = 18 → x = 3, y = 2

Multiply every term, including the constant, when you scale an equation.

Word Problems

Define the variable → write the equation → solve → answer the question asked, with units.

WordsMath
5 more than twice a number2n + 5
7 less than a numbern − 7
flat fee plus rate per unitfee + rate × units
count and value (two unknowns)a + c = total; price·a + price·c = dollars

Whole-number answers: "at most" usually rounds down; "at least" usually rounds up. Test your number.

Top mistakes: distributing to only the first term; forgetting to flip (or flipping when the divisor is positive); not multiplying every term by the LCD; subtracting a fee you should have added (or the reverse); answering for the wrong variable; checking only one equation of a system.
